skills.name: Remote access planning (VNC/RDP/SSH)
skills.description: Choose how to control a PC remotely — SSH, RDP or VNC/TightVNC remote desktop — matching the goal to the safest path.
skills.instructions:
Workflow:
1. Clarify the goal: full GUI desktop (RDP/VNC), terminal only (SSH), or one single app.
2. Check what the target runs: Windows (built-in RDP, TightVNC optional), macOS (Screen Sharing = VNC, SSH via Remote Login), Linux (SSH plus x11vnc/TigerVNC).
3. Map the network path: LAN direct, VPN, SSH tunnel, or router port forward. Never expose raw VNC or RDP ports directly to the internet.
4. Prefer in this order: SSH, then RDP with NLA, then VNC wrapped in an SSH tunnel.
5. Verify reachability with net.portscan before advising: 22 (SSH), 3389 (RDP), 5900 (VNC).
6. Record the chosen path and where credentials live with memory.save for future sessions.

skills.name: Remote host connectivity diagnostics
skills.description: Diagnose an unreachable remote PC or server — ping, port and firewall checks for VNC, RDP and SSH connections.
skills.instructions:
Workflow:
1. Confirm the exact address/IP the user is connecting to; a wrong IP explains most false alarms.
2. Reachability: process.exec ping the host. If it fails, check the local subnet/ARP first, then routing.
3. Port checks with net.portscan: 22 (SSH), 3389 (RDP), 5900 (VNC). A closed port does not mean the host is down.
4. Distinguish three failures: port open but auth rejected, port filtered by a firewall, host actually down.
5. If another path to the target exists, verify the service is running and listening on 0.0.0.0 (not 127.0.0.1), and that its host firewall allows the port.
6. Retest from a second vantage point (mobile tethering) to rule out ISP or router blocking.
7. Report as: host status, port status, most likely cause, next concrete fix.

skills.name: SSH tunneling for VNC and RDP
skills.description: Tunnel VNC or RDP through SSH so remote desktop sessions stay encrypted end to end.
skills.instructions:
Workflow:
1. Preconditions: SSH access to some host on the target network — the PC itself, or the MikroTik/pfSense box acting as jump host.
2. VNC through the tunnel: process.exec ssh -N -L 5900:TARGET_IP:5900 user@SSH_HOST
3. RDP through the tunnel: process.exec ssh -N -L 3389:TARGET_IP:3389 user@SSH_HOST (use a free local port like 13389 if 3389 is busy on the phone).
4. Keep -N (no remote shell); add -f to background the tunnel once it works.
5. Point the VNC/RDP client at localhost:LOCAL_PORT — traffic is now encrypted even though stock VNC is plaintext.
6. Verify the local listener with net.portscan against 127.0.0.1 on the chosen port.
7. Never expose 5900/3389 directly to the internet; the tunnel IS the security boundary.
8. Close tunnels when done: kill the ssh process with system.process_kill.

skills.name: RDP exposure review
skills.description: Review RDP (Remote Desktop) exposure and settings on a Windows PC or server before enabling remote access.
skills.instructions:
Workflow:
1. Inventory: which machines answer on 3389 (net.portscan); is any of them internet-facing?
2. Settings to verify on the target (via SSH/PowerShell or by guiding the user): Network Level Authentication ON, only required accounts in the Remote Desktop Users group, built-in Administrator renamed or protected.
3. Confirm the listener uses TLS; for older Windows versions, web.search the specific hardening steps (protocols and cipher order).
4. If internet-facing: recommend VPN or SSH tunnel access instead (skill: SSH tunneling for VNC and RDP), or at minimum a pfSense/MikroTik firewall rule limiting source IPs.
5. Check for brute-force pressure where logs are reachable: bursts of failed logons (Windows Event ID 4625).
6. Summarize exposure as direct internet / LAN-only / tunneled, plus a prioritized fix list.

skills.name: VNC / TightVNC security review
skills.description: Audit a VNC or TightVNC server — password, encryption, port exposure — before trusting it for remote desktop control.
skills.instructions:
Workflow:
1. Find VNC servers: net.portscan for 5900 (and 5800 for the Java/HTTP viewer some builds expose).
2. Authentication: is a password set at all (no-auth VNC is common on LANs and dangerous)? Note the legacy 8-character VNC password limit — recommend the longest password the client allows.
3. Encryption: stock VNC protocol is plaintext; TightVNC 2.x protects the auth handshake but screen data may still be readable — recommend wrapping in SSH (skill: SSH tunneling for VNC and RDP).
4. Limit who may connect: TightVNC access-control IP lists, or router firewall rules permitting only management subnets.
5. Least privilege: run the server without admin rights when possible; use view-only mode where input control is not needed.
6. Report: exposure (LAN or internet), auth state, encryption state, and the three highest-priority fixes.

skills.name: Remote session troubleshooting
skills.description: Fix flaky remote desktop sessions — VNC disconnects, RDP black screens, lag and login failures.
skills.instructions:
Workflow:
1. Classify the symptom: cannot connect at all (use the connectivity diagnostics skill), connects then drops, or connects but looks broken.
2. Connects-then-drops: check for duplicate IP on the LAN, power saving on the PC (sleep kills VNC), and MTU problems on VPN paths.
3. RDP black screen: the user is logged in at the physical console — log out the local session or detach the console session, then reconnect.
4. Lag: run process.exec ping continuously during a session; sustained loss above 1-2 percent explains most bad sessions; prefer wired or strong Wi-Fi over mobile data.
5. Auth failures: check caps lock and domain prefix, then password expiry; for VNC verify the server password was not changed by an update.
6. After fixing, complete a full connect cycle and record the root cause with memory.save.

skills.name: RouterOS health check (SSH)
skills.description: Health-check a MikroTik RouterOS router over SSH — CPU, memory, interfaces, logs and routes.
skills.instructions:
Workflow:
1. Connect: process.exec ssh admin@ROUTER_IP (the bundled ssh client works with RouterOS). Confirm platform and version: /system resource print
2. Health: /system resource print for CPU load and free memory; /system health print for voltage and temperature where the board supports it.
3. Interfaces: /interface print for link state and error counters; /interface monitor-traffic once for live throughput.
4. Logs: /log print without-paging — scan for criticals, interface flaps and repeated login failures.
5. Routes: /ip route print — verify the default route exists and is not blackholed.
6. Capacity: /file print for free storage before any upgrade or backup work.
7. Summarize as a table: resources, interface errors, log alerts, route health. Flag CPU above 80 percent, memory below 10 percent free, or repeated auth failures.

skills.name: Safe Mode change discipline
skills.description: Change MikroTik RouterOS config without lockout risk using Safe Mode on every risky router change.
skills.instructions:
Workflow:
1. Before ANY config change enter Safe Mode: press Ctrl-X in the SSH/console session — the prompt shows [Safe Mode is activated]. In WinBox, tick Safe Mode.
2. Make changes in small batches. Keep a second SSH login open to test connectivity while the first session holds Safe Mode.
3. If you lose access or break something: a dead safe-mode session rolls everything back automatically — reconnect, diagnose, re-plan.
4. Commit changes: press Ctrl-X again to exit Safe Mode and keep them (in WinBox, untick Safe Mode). Closing a safe-mode session without committing reverts it.
5. Undo after committing: /system history print to see changes and revert from there, or restore a backup (skill: Backup and export discipline).
6. Never paste large scripts into a live session outside Safe Mode; rehearse inside Safe Mode first.

skills.name: Backup and export discipline
skills.description: Back up a MikroTik router — binary backup plus text export — and keep copies off the RouterOS device.
skills.instructions:
Workflow:
1. Always take BOTH formats: binary backup (full restore, same hardware) and readable export: /system backup save name=before-change and /export file=before-change
2. Encrypt backups that contain secrets: /system backup save name=before-change password=SECRET
3. Pull copies off the device: /file print to confirm, then process.exec scp admin@ROUTER_IP:before-change.backup . — a backup only on the router is not a backup.
4. For change review, export selectively as text: /export terse or per-area exports like /ip firewall export
5. Automate: /system scheduler running a daily backup script (skill: Scripting and schedulers) plus an off-box upload or email step.
6. After any major change take a fresh pair; verify files exist with non-zero size, and test-restore on a lab CHR or spare unit when possible.

skills.name: RouterOS firewall review
skills.description: Review MikroTik RouterOS firewall and NAT rules for holes, dead rules and unsafe port forwards.
skills.instructions:
Workflow:
1. Dump the rules: /ip firewall filter print detail and /ip firewall nat print detail; save the output with file.write for structured review.
2. Input chain (traffic to the router): must drop what is not needed; winbox (8291) and ssh (22) must be restricted to management subnets via address lists.
3. Forward chain: verify established/related accept rules sit near the top and hunt for broad accept-all rules.
4. NAT: flag any dst-nat port forward from WAN to RDP 3389, VNC 5900 or winbox 8291 — these belong behind VPN instead (skill: RouterOS VPN setup).
5. Find dead rules: anything placed after a broader matching drop never fires — count and report them.
6. Recommend the classic base if missing: drop invalid, accept established/related, drop new input from WAN not dstnatted, allow management only from listed subnets.
7. Apply changes only in Safe Mode (skill: Safe Mode change discipline).

skills.name: RouterOS hardening baseline
skills.description: Harden a MikroTik RouterOS device — services, users, management access and RouterOS updates.
skills.instructions:
Workflow:
1. Services: /ip service print — disable telnet, ftp and www if unused; restrict the rest: /ip service set winbox address=10.0.0.0/24 (adjust to the management subnet).
2. Users: /user print — create a named admin, then remove or demote the default admin account; assign least-privilege groups.
3. Update RouterOS: /system package update check-for-updates then download-and-install (announce the reboot; do it in Safe Mode). Also update routerboard firmware if /system routerboard print shows an upgrade pending.
4. Leak prevention: /ip neighbor discovery-settings set discover-interface-list=!WAN and restrict /tool mac-server to LAN interfaces.
5. SSH crypto: /ip ssh set strong-crypto=yes; prefer key-based auth for new setups.
6. Verify afterwards: net.portscan the router — only 22 and 8291 (from LAN) should answer, nothing from WAN.
7. Document the baseline applied and any deviations with memory.save.

skills.name: RouterOS VPN (WireGuard/IPsec) setup
skills.description: Set up or fix a VPN on MikroTik RouterOS — WireGuard, IPsec or L2TP — for secure remote access.
skills.instructions:
Workflow:
1. Prefer WireGuard on RouterOS v7: /interface wireguard add name=wg0 listen-port=13231 — note the generated public key.
2. One peer per device: /interface wireguard peers add interface=wg0 public-key=PEER_KEY allowed-address=10.10.10.2/32
3. Address and routing: /ip address add interface=wg0 address=10.10.10.1/24; the peer allowed-address must cover its tunnel IP.
4. Firewall: accept UDP 13231 on the input chain from WAN; put wg0 in a trusted interface list and allow its subnet through the forward chain.
5. IPsec/IKEv2 or L2TP only when a client requires it (e.g. Windows built-in) — it is heavier to configure; keep the policy, peer and identity trio consistent.
6. Client config: supply [Interface] and [Peer] blocks with Endpoint set to the router WAN IP or DDNS name and the right AllowedIPs.
7. Verify both directions: ping across the tunnel, then check handshake freshness in /interface wireguard peers print.
8. Changes go through Safe Mode (skill: Safe Mode change discipline).

skills.name: Wireless tuning (2.4/5 GHz)
skills.description: Tune MikroTik Wi-Fi — channels, bands and security — to fix weak signal and drops on 2.4 and 5 GHz.
skills.instructions:
Workflow:
1. Survey before changing: /interface wireless scan (legacy) or /interface wifi scan (v7 wifi-qcom) — pick the least congested channel.
2. 2.4 GHz: use only channels 1, 6 or 11 at 20 MHz width. 5 GHz: prefer 36-48 or 149-165; DFS channels can delay startup on some clients.
3. Security: WPA2-PSK minimum, WPA3 where all clients support it; never WEP or open networks.
4. Power: do not max TX power — it creates one-way links; defaults are usually right.
5. Client view: /interface wireless registration-table print — signals worse than about -70 dBm need AP repositioning, not settings changes.
6. Detect the menu first: v7 boards with the wifi package use /interface wifi syntax — do not guess commands across the two stacks.
7. After changes, re-test throughput and roaming; on multi-AP setups coordinate through CAPsMAN.

skills.name: QoS and queue management
skills.description: Shape bandwidth on MikroTik with queues — fix bufferbloat, prioritize VoIP and keep latency low.
skills.instructions:
Workflow:
1. Measure first: upload and download capacity while idle. Queue only at the true bottleneck, normally the WAN interface.
2. Bufferbloat check: run process.exec ping during a speed test; latency jumping more than about 50 ms means shaping is needed.
3. Start simple: /queue simple with max-limit set to about 90 percent of measured rates, separate entries for up and down.
4. Fairness: use pcq or sfq queue types so one client cannot starve the rest.
5. Priorities: mark VoIP, DNS and interactive traffic with mangle rules, then give their queues higher priority in a /queue tree design (voip=1, dns=2, interactive=5, bulk=8).
6. Verify: re-run ping-under-load; latency should stay near baseline — lower max-limit until it does.
7. Save measured baselines and the queue design with memory.save.

skills.name: Scripting and schedulers
skills.description: Automate MikroTik RouterOS with scripts and schedulers — backups, watchdogs, dynamic block lists.
skills.instructions:
Workflow:
1. Define the job precisely: trigger (schedule or event), exact action, and what happens on failure.
2. Write it: /system script add name=daily-backup source='/system backup save name=auto; /export file=auto' — quote sources containing spaces or semicolons.
3. Schedule: /system scheduler add name=daily-backup interval=1d on-event=daily-backup start-time=03:00:00
4. Test immediately: /system script run daily-backup then confirm outputs in /file print.
5. Common automations: nightly off-box backup push, netwatch WAN monitors with notifications, dynamic address-list block feeds, CPU or temperature alerts into the log.
6. Error handling: wrap network-dependent steps in :do {} on-error={} and log outcomes at key points.
7. Keep scripts idempotent — safe to re-run with no duplicate side effects.

skills.name: pfSense status check
skills.description: Health-check a pfSense firewall — interfaces, gateways, state table, load and logs.
skills.instructions:
Workflow:
1. Access: SSH to the firewall (console option 8 gives a shell) or use Diagnostics > Command Prompt in the web UI.
2. Interfaces: ifconfig -a on the shell or the dashboard — WAN must have a live address; look for repeated carrier flaps on any port.
3. Gateways: Status > Gateways (dpinger data) — packet loss or latency on WAN explains most internet-down reports.
4. State table: pfctl -si for usage versus limits; pfctl -ss | wc -l for the live count.
5. Load: top on the shell — interrupt CPU from Suricata, dpinger or high pps is the usual suspect.
6. Logs: Status > System Logs — filter for errors, gateway alarms and VPN renegotiation spam.
7. Verdict: report interface, gateway, state-table, load and log findings, each marked healthy or not, with the top issue first.

skills.name: pfSense change safety (config.xml, rollback)
skills.description: Edit pfSense safely — config.xml backup, rollback plan and a live console session before risky changes.
skills.instructions:
Workflow:
1. Back up first: Diagnostics > Backup & Restore to download config.xml; on the shell: cp /conf/config.xml /conf/backup/ then scp it off-box.
2. Plan the change as one atomic unit: list every rule, alias and setting that will be touched.
3. Apply one logical change at a time and verify with a real client test before the next.
4. Keep an SSH or console session open during risky changes; if the web UI breaks, the console menu still works.
5. Rollback paths: Diagnostics > Backup & Restore > Restore, console option 15 (restore recent configuration), or shell: copy the chosen /conf/backup/config-*.xml back to /conf/config.xml and run /etc/rc.reload_all
6. Hand edits to /conf/config.xml are overwritten by the UI — always change settings through the UI or console.
7. Export the config.xml off-site after every successful change session; it is the single source of truth.

skills.name: Firewall rule design (least privilege)
skills.description: Design pfSense firewall rules with least privilege — aliases, rule order, logging and floating rules.
skills.instructions:
Workflow:
1. Inventory what must talk to what: LAN subnets, servers, management hosts, guest and IoT zones.
2. Aliases first (Firewall > Aliases): named host and port aliases make rules readable and auditable.
3. Order matters: rules evaluate top-down, first match wins — specific allows above broad ones on each interface.
4. Default posture: LAN allow-all is normal at home; for shared networks replace it with explicit allows (DNS, NTP, HTTP/S) and log the catch-all block.
5. Floating rules: keep to a minimum — with Quick set they match before interface rules and confuse debugging.
6. Log selectively: enable logging on denies that matter; logging everything hides real events in noise.
7. Never manage pfSense from WAN; restrict 443 and 22 to an alias of named management hosts.
8. After applying, confirm behavior with Diagnostics > pfTOP and state formation on the new rules.

skills.name: NAT and port forwarding review
skills.description: Review pfSense NAT and port forwards — find risky internet exposures and replace them with VPN access.
skills.instructions:
Workflow:
1. List forwards: Firewall > NAT > Port Forward — for each note source restriction, destination port and internal target.
2. Flag high-risk WAN forwards: RDP 3389, VNC 5900, router admin 80/443/22, SMB 445 (never), camera or NVR web UIs. Replace with VPN access (skill: VPN on pfSense).
3. Check each forward has its associated firewall rule with a restricted source; a forward open to any source targeting an admin service is an incident waiting to happen.
4. Outbound NAT: the default hybrid mode is fine; custom manual rules can break VoIP and VPN — verify before editing.
5. NAT reflection: enable only if LAN clients truly must use the public IP; prefer split-DNS instead.
6. Verify from outside after changes: net.portscan against the WAN IP from a tethered phone — only intended ports may answer.
7. Document every surviving forward: purpose, user, review date.

skills.name: VPN on pfSense (WireGuard/IPsec/OpenVPN)
skills.description: Set up or fix VPN on pfSense — WireGuard, IPsec/IKEv2 or OpenVPN — and verify remote tunnels.
skills.instructions:
Workflow:
1. Prefer WireGuard: VPN > WireGuard, create the interface, assign it under Interfaces, set the listen port (51820), add peers with their allowed IPs.
2. Firewall for WireGuard: accept UDP 51820 on WAN; add rules ON the wg interface itself to reach LAN resources — WG traffic arrives on its own interface, not LAN.
3. IPsec/IKEv2 for native OS clients: mobile clients with EAP or certificates; only if WireGuard is not workable for the fleet.
4. OpenVPN for maximum compatibility: use the wizard, TLS plus user auth, and DCO where supported.
5. Verify: Status > WireGuard for handshakes, Status > IPsec for tunnels, Status > OpenVPN for connected clients.
6. Test from outside: connect a phone client, ping a LAN IP, confirm DNS works (push the pfSense LAN IP as DNS).
7. Common breakage: missing wg-interface rules, overlapping allowed-addresses, MTU — if SSH works but web pages hang, lower MSS/MTU on the tunnel.

skills.name: Packages and IDS (Suricata, pfBlockerNG)
skills.description: Run pfSense packages well — Suricata IDS/IPS and pfBlockerNG — without drowning in false positives.
skills.instructions:
Workflow:
1. Start read-only: Services > Suricata in IDS (alert-only) mode for one to two weeks; tune before you ever block.
2. Rulesets: enable only ET open categories relevant to services you actually expose; alerts for services you do not run are pure noise.
3. Review the Alerts tab daily at first; suppress legitimate traffic with suppress lists rather than disabling whole categories.
4. Promote to IPS (inline blocking) only after tuning; inline mode needs supported NICs and adds latency.
5. pfBlockerNG: start with default IP and DNS feeds; read its reports before adding aggressive lists that break legitimate sites.
6. Resources: Suricata struggles on boxes with under 2 GB RAM — check top before and after enabling.
7. Record tuning decisions (feeds chosen, suppressions) with memory.save so later sessions do not re-litigate them.

skills.name: Traffic shaping and limiters
skills.description: Fix bufferbloat on pfSense with limiters and FQ-CoDel shaping — keep latency flat under load.
skills.instructions:
Workflow:
1. Measure baseline: ping a stable IP during a full speed test; inflation above about 30-50 ms means bufferbloat and shaping is justified.
2. Modern approach: Limiters (Firewall > Traffic Shaper > Limiters) with FQ-CoDel discipline, set to 90-95 percent of measured upload and download rates.
3. Apply with a floating quick rule on WAN: in-direction traffic to the download limiter, out-direction to the upload limiter; leave ICMP unshaped for honest tests.
4. VoIP priority: either the shaper wizard VOIP preset or a higher-priority child queue; prove it with a call during a big download.
5. Per-host fairness: enable source/destination mask on limiters so a single client cannot consume everything.
6. Verify: re-run ping-under-load; latency should sit near baseline — adjust percentages until it holds.
7. Save measured ISP rates and the date with memory.save; ISP speeds drift and shaping must track them.

skills.name: Troubleshooting with pfctl, states, packet capture
skills.description: Debug blocked traffic on pfSense — packet captures, pfctl state inspection, gateway and DNS checks.
skills.instructions:
Workflow:
1. Localize the failure: client to pfSense (rule hit), pfSense to internet (gateway or DNS), or server-side.
2. Rule trace: Firewall > Log View filtered by client IP and port — a blocked entry names the exact rule that denied it.
3. No log entry means traffic never arrived: run Diagnostics > Packet Capture on WAN and LAN interfaces with the client IP as filter and compare both sides.
4. Live view: Diagnostics > pfTOP for real-time states; on the shell pfctl -ss filtered by the IP confirms established state.
5. Uplink checks: Status > Gateways for loss/latency; on the shell drill example.com @8.8.8.8 separates DNS failures from routing failures.
6. After any rule fix, clear stale states for the affected host (Diagnostics > States, filtered reset) — broken long-lived states survive rule changes.
7. Close with: root cause, the exact log line that proved it, and whether the fix is permanent or a workaround.

skills.name: Upgrade discipline and recovery
skills.description: Upgrade pfSense safely — pre-flight checks, correct update path and recovery if it fails.
skills.instructions:
Workflow:
1. Pre-flight: download config.xml off-box (skill: pfSense change safety), note installed packages (they can lag new releases), check System > Update for the target version.
2. Read the release notes for the exact version (web.search pfSense release notes) — breaking changes and package removals are listed there.
3. Schedule a maintenance window: upgrades reboot the firewall and expect 5-15 minutes of outage.
4. Path: upgrade one release at a time rather than skipping several; keep CE and Plus channels consistent with the installed product.
5. If it hangs: wait up to 30 minutes; then use the console — option 15 to restore the pre-upgrade configuration, or reinstall from media and restore the saved config.xml.
6. Post-upgrade verification: dashboard, gateway status, VPN tunnels re-handshaking, package versions, and a config diff against the pre-upgrade export.
7. Keep the pre-upgrade config.xml for at least a stable week before pruning old backups.
